chapter_theme: A song at Thirumanthurai (திருமாந்துறை): the poet pictures old age, bent body, loose teeth, cough, bedridden years and fading sense, and asks Murugan to come on the peacock before life goes and give his planted feet; the praise names Valli's millet field and the mango-rich fields of the shrine.

899.reading: The poet pictures the body bent, the teeth loose, the mind faltering, years passing on the bed, a cough, a swollen aching belly and sense fading, and asks that before life goes Murugan come on the high peacock and give his firmly planted feet. The praise names Murugan the bridegroom of Valli in the sweet millet field with its vengai trees, who grants those who seek him states beyond what they hold, and the lord of the fertile land where ripe mangoes burst and flow into the paddy fields, at Manthurai where men and the king of the gods praise him.
899.nuance: The decline is told in a short run of verbs (வளைந்து, நெகிழ்ந்து, தடுமாறி, நொந்து, ஓய்ந்து, அழிந்து). ஆர்ந்துள கடன்கள் வாங்கவும் அறிந்து may mean knowing how to collect what is owed, the old man's mind still on debts; the reading is uncertain. மாங்கனி உடைந்து தேங்க: a play on the shrine's name, mango ford.

links.note: Kural 335 says good deeds must be done before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 899 pictures the same last stage, cough, swollen belly, sense fading, and asks Murugan to come on the peacock and give his feet before life goes (உயிர்போமுன்). Both fix the deadline at the body's last failing; the Kural puts the work on the person, the song puts it on the god.
